summary:
SoilMate is a satellite-driven information dashboard platform made for farmers to monitor rainfall, air temperature, relative humidity, crop sunlight exposure, soil conditions, and plant stress levels. The dashboard is built around smallholder farmers across Malaysia based on the case study in the Kulai-Skudai-Pontian agro-corridor of Southern Johor.

To address the Field Shift challenge, we replace delayed, rainfall-only alerts with a 4-Layer Agro-Climate Risk Assessment Framework powered by open-access NASA POWER and SMAP Level-4 observation data. Rather than waiting for visible crop wilting, the platform tracks four sequential physical triggers:

1. 14-day cumulative precipitation deficits (CPD14)
2. Spikes in atmospheric vapor pressure deficit (VPD)
3. Critical root-zone moisture depletion (0-100 cm GWETROOT percentiles)
4. Plant stress (Evaporative Stress Index)

When risk escalates, SoilMate automatically identifies vulnerable planting windows and outputs actionable, deep-rooted crop-rotation advisories tailored to local Malaysian crops like Kulai chilli, sweetcorn, and tropical legumes.

In humid tropical regions like Southeast Asia, flash droughts deplete root-zone soil moisture up to three times faster than the global average, causing 15%–20% yield losses for rainfed smallholders who lack field sensors. SoilMate translates free NASA satellite data into timely, farm-level decisions that protect yields and rural livelihoods.
details:
What does our project do?

SoilMate is a satellite-driven early-warning dashboard that helps smallholder farmers in Malaysia spot a flash drought before their crops start to wilt. It covers all 13 states and 3 Federal Territories, with a case study in the Kulai–Skudai–Pontian farming corridor of Southern Johor. A farmer picks their state and a date, and the dashboard shows:

  • Overall Agriculture Risk: one alert level (Normal, Watch, Warning or Flash Drought), the alert level out of 3, and a short line of advice.
  • Good time to plant?: a Yes or No answer backed by three simple checks: soil moisture, recent rain and recent warnings.
  • Weather today: maximum temperature, humidity, rain and wind.
  • Crop & soil simulation: an illustrated crop and soil scene that changes with the data. A time selector (3 weeks ago → 2 weeks ago → 1 week ago → Selected date) lets farmers watch a dry spell build up.
  • Four layer cards: Rainfall deficit, Air dryness, Soil moisture and Plant stress, each with a plain-language verdict such as “Very little rain” or “Roots have enough water”.
  • Malaysia risk map: an interactive map with five views: Overall alert, Rainfall, Air dryness, Soil moisture and Plant stress.
  • Risk by layer: how much each layer contributes to the overall risk.
  • Monitoring & Analysis page: charts over 14, 30 or 90 days (Rainfall balance, Dry-air pressure, Water around the roots and Plant response) for extension officers, agronomists and judges.

How does our project work?

Most drought alerts look at rainfall alone, so they react late. SoilMate follows a flash drought through four layers instead, in the order it actually happens. Each layer is compared with that location’s own NASA record from 2001 to 2025.

  • Layer 1 – Rainfall deficit (CPD14): daily NASA POWER rainfall (PRECTOTCORR) is added up over 14 days and compared with the normal amount for those dates. 14-day totals filter out noise from short tropical downpours.
  • Layer 2 – Air dryness (VPD and sunlight): vapour pressure deficit (VPD, in kPa) is calculated from maximum temperature (T2M_MAX) and humidity (RH2M), together with sunlight (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN). A day above the local 90th percentile is flagged as unusually hot and dry.
  • Layer 3 – Soil moisture: root-zone wetness (GWETROOT, 0–100 cm) and topsoil wetness (GWETTOP, 0–5 cm) are turned into percentiles and cross-checked against SMAP Level-4 root-zone soil moisture.
  • Layer 4 – Plant stress: the ECOSTRESS Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) shows whether crops are actually struggling to move water.

Flash drought rule: we follow Ford & Labosier (2017). A flash drought starts when root-zone soil moisture falls from the 40th percentile or higher to below the 20th percentile within 20 days. SoilMate only raises the alert if rain is also at least 25% below normal, which cuts false alarms. The event is confirmed once it lasts 15 days.

The four layers combine into one alert level:

  • Normal: no warning signs.
  • Watch: one early sign, such as rain 25% below normal, unusually dry air, topsoil losing 15% of its water in 3 days, or root-zone soil below the 30th percentile.
  • Warning: signs appearing together, such as a rain shortage while root-zone soil is below the 30th percentile.
  • Flash Drought: the flash drought rule above is met.

Real example (Perlis, 31 December 2025): rain was 82% below normal (“Very little rain”), but the air was normal (1.1 kPa), the roots had enough water (67th percentile) and the plants were healthy. Only the rainfall layer raised a sign, so the level was Watch (1 of 3). Risk by layer showed rainfall at 82%, against 4–5% for each of the other layers. Good time to plant? said No, because the rain check failed.

System architecture:

  • Data preparation: Python scripts download NASA POWER through its API, and SMAP, ECOSTRESS and IMERG through NASA Earthdata and AppEEARS, then clean and align the data together with partner data.
  • Project data store: CSV and GeoJSON files hold the daily layers, the 2001–2025 baselines and the Malaysia state boundaries.
  • Web application: a Python FastAPI app with Jinja2 templates runs the 4-layer risk engine.
  • Web dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Bootstrap, Plotly.js charts and a Leaflet map.
  • Hosting: the app runs on a team server and is published to the web through a Cloudflare Tunnel, so anyone can open it in a browser.

How does our project benefit farmers?

  • No field hardware: farmers don’t need soil probes or a weather station, only a phone, tablet or laptop with a web browser.
  • Earlier action: soil moisture and air dryness change before leaves wilt or satellite greenness (NDVI) drops. That gives farmers days to weeks to water, delay planting or protect young plants.
  • Less wasted seed and fertiliser: the planting check stops farmers sowing into dry seedbeds, or planting too early after one short shower.
  • Plain language: every number comes with an everyday verdict, such as “Very little rain”, “Roots have enough water” or “Plants are healthy”.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Flash droughts are most likely in humid and semi-humid regions, including Southeast Asia. A global satellite study found that a third to almost half of them now develop within five days (Qing et al., 2022, Nature Communications), which gives rainfed smallholders very little time to react. Water shortages already cost Malaysian agriculture. For oil palm, every extra 100 mm of soil water deficit cuts yield by about 10%, and the 2015/16 El Niño drought cut Malaysia’s palm oil production by 8%.

SoilMate aims to give smallholders the kind of early warning that large plantations get from their own sensors, so they can protect yields, waste less seed and fertiliser, and strengthen rural food security. The next step is to move from drought alerts to smarter crop choices, with crop-specific thresholds and crop choice and rotation advice for local crops such as Kulai chilli, sweetcorn and tropical legumes.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used to develop the project?

NASA data

  • NASA POWER (MERRA-2 / CERES): daily rainfall, temperature, humidity, sunlight and soil wetness for all four layers
  • SMAP Level-4 (SPL4SMGP): root-zone soil moisture check
  • ECOSTRESS (ECO_L4T_ESI): Evaporative Stress Index for plant stress
  • GPM IMERG: second source for rainfall
  • AppEEARS and NASA Earthdata: finding, downloading and cutting the data down to Malaysia

Space agency partner and other data

  • NOAA Climate Prediction Center and Physical Sciences Laboratory: regional climate context
  • OpenDOSM (Department of Statistics Malaysia) and FAO: Malaysian crop and production statistics
  • geoBoundaries (via the Humanitarian Data Exchange): Malaysia state boundaries for the map

Software

  • Python for data preparation, with a FastAPI web application and Jinja2 templates running the 4-layer risk engine
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Bootstrap and the Inter font for the dashboard
  • Plotly.js for interactive charts and Leaflet for the Malaysia risk map
  • CSV and GeoJSON files for the project data
  • Cloudflare Tunnel to publish the prototype to the web
  • Automated tests in Python

Hardware

  • Standard laptops for development. We tested the dashboard on desktop, tablet and phone screens down to 320 px wide.

AI tools

  • Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex for literature review, code prototyping, refining the layout and structuring the risk layers. The team reviewed and tested everything these tools produced.

How is our project creative?

  • A crop and soil scene that “feels” the weather: instead of tables, farmers see an illustrated scene whose sky, soil and plants change with the four layers. They can step back three weeks to watch a dry spell build.
  • Science translated, not hidden: from the same data, the Overview page speaks plain language to farmers, while the Monitoring & Analysis page shows the detailed trends for experts.
  • Local thresholds: each alert compares a location with its own 25-year history (percentiles) instead of using one fixed number for the whole country.
  • Risk by layer: farmers and officers can see which layer is driving the risk, such as rain in the Perlis example, so the advice is easy to trust.
  • Five-view risk map: one map switches between Overall alert, Rainfall, Air dryness, Soil moisture and Plant stress across all 16 states and federal territories.

What factors were considered?

  • Farmers who aren’t scientists: there’s no jargon on the main page. It uses large, readable numbers, a colour plus words for every status, and a Pause motion control on the animated simulation.
  • Tropical cloud cover: satellites that photograph the ground often can’t see through Malaysia’s clouds. We rely on gap-free NASA POWER data and SMAP soil moisture, whose microwave signal passes through cloud, and we show when the last clear-sky ECOSTRESS reading was taken.
  • Noisy rainfall: we use 14-day totals instead of single days, and the flash drought rule also requires a rain shortage.
  • Data resolution: each NASA POWER grid cell is roughly 50 km wide, so SoilMate gives area-level guidance rather than single-field measurements.
  • Different climates across Malaysia: because the rules use percentiles, the same rules work from Perlis to Sabah.
  • Honest data checks: where a dataset still needs checking, the dashboard says so, for example the “ESI scale needs review” note for Johor.
  • Low cost: free, open NASA data and a browser-based dashboard, with no paid services or extra hardware for farmers.
